claims.claim: i-CDK9 markedly reduced the CDK9-mediated pSer2 in the Pol II CTD in a dose-dependent manner in HeLa cells
claims.source: Consistent with its specific binding to and potent inhibition of purified CDK9-CycT1 in vitro, i-CDK9 markedly reduced the CDK9-mediated pSer2 in the Pol II CTD and Thr775 (pThr775) in the DSIF subunit SPT5 in a dose-dependent manner in HeLa cells (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The dose-dependent reduction is shown by Western blotting in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: i-CDK9 markedly reduced Thr775 phosphorylation in the DSIF subunit SPT5 in a dose-dependent manner in HeLa cells
claims.source: Consistent with its specific binding to and potent inhibition of purified CDK9-CycT1 in vitro, i-CDK9 markedly reduced the CDK9-mediated pSer2 in the Pol II CTD and Thr775 (pThr775) in the DSIF subunit SPT5 in a dose-dependent manner in HeLa cells (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The dose-dependent reduction is shown by Western blotting in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: i-CDK9 markedly down-regulated the expression of the short-lived anti-apoptotic protein MCL-1
claims.source: Indeed, correlating with the decrease in cellular levels of pSer2 and pThr775, i-CDK9 markedly down-regulated the expression of the short-lived anti-apoptotic protein MCL-1 and at the same time induced proteolytic cleavage of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), which is considered a major hallmark of apoptosis and caspase activation (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The down-regulation is shown by Western blotting in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: i-CDK9 induced proteolytic cleavage of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP)
claims.source: Indeed, correlating with the decrease in cellular levels of pSer2 and pThr775, i-CDK9 markedly down-regulated the expression of the short-lived anti-apoptotic protein MCL-1 and at the same time induced proteolytic cleavage of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), which is considered a major hallmark of apoptosis and caspase activation (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The PARP cleavage is shown by Western blotting in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Proteolytic cleavage of PARP is considered a major hallmark of apoptosis and caspase activation
claims.source: Indeed, correlating with the decrease in cellular levels of pSer2 and pThr775, i-CDK9 markedly down-regulated the expression of the short-lived anti-apoptotic protein MCL-1 and at the same time induced proteolytic cleavage of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), which is considered a major hallmark of apoptosis and caspase activation (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Among the total of 11,197 genes with detectable Pol II peaks, 7805 (70%) showed a traveling ratio (TR) greater than 2.0 in the control DMSO-treated HeLa cells
claims.source: Similar to the situation reported in other cell types (Zeitlinger et al., 2007; Rahl et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2013), among the total of 11,197 genes with detectable Pol peaks, 7805 (70%) showed a traveling ratio (TR; also called the pausing index; (Zeitlinger et al., 2007; Rahl et al., 2010) greater than 2.0 in the control DMSO-treated HeLa cells.
claims.evidence: The TR values are calculated from ChIP-seq data and compared to published findings in other cell types.

claims.claim: Upon treatment with i-CDK9 for 2 hr, 6339 (56.6%) genes displayed an increase of at least 1.5-fold in Pol II TR
claims.source: Importantly, upon treatment with i-CDK9 for 2 and 8 hr, 6339 (56.6%) and 7658 (68.4%) genes displayed an increase of at least 1.5-fold in Pol II TR, respectively (Figure 2B)
claims.evidence: The TR changes are determined by ChIP-seq analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Upon treatment with i-CDK9 for 8 hr, 7658 (68.4%) genes displayed an increase of at least 1.5-fold in Pol II TR
claims.source: Importantly, upon treatment with i-CDK9 for 2 and 8 hr, 6339 (56.6%) and 7658 (68.4%) genes displayed an increase of at least 1.5-fold in Pol II TR, respectively (Figure 2B)
claims.evidence: The TR changes are determined by ChIP-seq analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The increase in Pol II TR upon i-CDK9 treatment indicates significantly elevated promoter-proximal pausing by Pol II upon CDK9 inhibition
claims.source: Importantly, upon treatment with i-CDK9 for 2 and 8 hr, 6339 (56.6%) and 7658 (68.4%) genes displayed an increase of at least 1.5-fold in Pol II TR, respectively (Figure 2B), indicating significantly elevated promoter-proximal pausing by Pol II upon CDK9 inhibition.
claims.evidence: The interpretation is based on the definition of TR and the ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: TR values for the 138 genes whose expression was up-regulated at least twofold by i-CDK9 were significantly less affected compared to the rest of the genes
claims.source: A comparison between the two data sets indicates that TR values for those 138 genes whose expression was up-regulated at least twofold by i-CDK9 were significantly less affected compared to the rest of the genes (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The comparison is made between ChIP-seq and microarray data, shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The top 4 gene sets with the largest increase in TR show an enrichment in biological processes ranging from RNA processing, DNA and non-coding RNA metabolic process to transcription
claims.source: Furthermore, the top 4 gene sets with the largest increase in TR show an enrichment in biological processes ranging from RNA processing, DNA and non-coding RNA metabolic process to transcription (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The enrichment is determined by GO analysis using DAVID and shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The top 4 gene sets whose expression had the biggest drop upon i-CDK9 treatment are populated by genes involved in regulation of transcription and RNA metabolic process
claims.source: Largely consistent with this TR-based analysis, the top 4 sets, whose expression had the biggest drop upon i-CDK9 treatment, are populated by genes involved in regulation of transcription and RNA metabolic process
claims.evidence: The enrichment is determined by GO analysis using DAVID.

claims.claim: Transcription regulation and RNA metabolic processes are particularly susceptible to inhibition of CDK9
claims.source: Largely consistent with this TR-based analysis, the top 4 sets, whose expression had the biggest drop upon i-CDK9 treatment, are populated by genes involved in regulation of transcription and RNA metabolic process, indicating that these processes and their control are particularly susceptible to inhibition of CDK9.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is based on the GO enrichment analysis of genes most affected by i-CDK9.

claims.claim: MYC expression in i-CDK9-treated HeLa cells displayed a biphasic response with a small initial decrease (within 2 hr) followed by a dramatic rebound (around 8 hr and continue at 16 hr)
claims.source: Microarray analysis performed at three different time points (2, 8 and 16 hr) indicates that MYC expression in i-CDK9-treated HeLa cells displayed an interesting biphasic responses with a small initial decrease (within 2 hr) followed by a dramatic rebound (around 8 hr and continue at 16 hr) in the presence of continuous CDK9 inhibition by i-CDK9 (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The biphasic response is shown by microarray analysis at multiple time points in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The biphasic MYC expression pattern in response to i-CDK9 was confirmed by qRT-PCR analysis
claims.source: This result was further confirmed by qRT-PCR analysis of MYC mRNA levels in cells treated with i-CDK9 or DMSO (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The confirmation is provided by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A similar biphasic MYC expression pattern was observed in four other cell lines (U87MG, A375, NCIH441, and A2058) representing a wide spectrum of human cancers and MYC amplification states
claims.source: In addition to HeLa cells, a similar biphasic expression pattern was also observed in four other cell lines representing a wide spectrum of human cancers and MYC amplification states (Figure 3A; http://www.broadinstitute.org/ccle/home).
claims.evidence: The biphasic pattern is shown by microarray analysis in multiple cell lines in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The extent of the initial decrease and subsequent induction of MYC mRNA production varied among the cell lines
claims.source: Notably, the extent of the initial decrease and then subsequent induction of MYC mRNA production varied among the cell lines.
claims.evidence: This observation is based on comparing the microarray data from different cell lines.

claims.claim: After 2 hr of i-CDK9 (0.5 µM) treatment, the MYC mRNA levels in U87MG and HeLa cells showed only a slight decrease compared to the DMSO control
claims.source: For example, after 2 hr of i-CDK9 (0.5 µM) treatment, the MYC mRNA levels in U87MG (MYC copy number [CN] = 2) and HeLa (CN = 4) cells showed only a slight decrease compared to the DMSO control
claims.evidence: This is shown by microarray analysis in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: After 2 hr of i-CDK9 (0.5 µM) treatment, MYC mRNA levels were significantly reduced in A375, NCIH441, and A2058 cells
claims.source: whereas they were significantly reduced in A375 (CN = 2), NCIH441 (CN = 8), and A2058 (CN = 4) cells.
claims.evidence: This is shown by microarray analysis in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Prolonged treatment for 8–16 hr caused the MYC mRNA to reach levels much higher than those in the control cells in all cell lines except NCIH441
claims.source: Furthermore, the prolonged treatment for 8–16 hr caused the MYC mRNA to reach levels much higher than those in the control cells in all cell lines except NCIH441 (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is shown by microarray analysis in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The induction of MYC expression in response to prolonged CDK9 inhibition by i-CDK9 is a general phenomenon likely caused by a common mechanism independent of the MYC amplification/expression levels
claims.source: Despite these variations, which could well be caused by differences in MYC mRNA stability in difference cell lines, it is clear that the induction of MYC expression in response to prolonged CDK9 inhibition by i-CDK9 is a general phenomenon likely caused by a common mechanism independent of the MYC amplification/expression levels.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation of similar patterns across multiple cell lines with different MYC copy numbers.

claims.claim: HEXIM1 was continuously suppressed throughout the entire 16 hr of i-CDK9 treatment in all five cell lines
claims.source: In contrast to MYC, another short-lived gene HEXIM1, which was previously shown to depend on active CDK9 for expression (He et al., 2006), was continuously suppressed throughout the entire 16 hr of i-CDK9 treatment in all five cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The continuous suppression is shown by microarray analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and the CDK9 dependence is supported by citation to He et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Upon exposure to 0.1 µM i-CDK9, the MYC level increased 3.6-fold whereas the global pSer2 level was only decreased by 23%
claims.source: Upon exposure to just 0.1 µM i-CDK9, the MYC level increased 3.6-fold whereas the global pSer2 level was only decreased by 23% (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The protein levels are measured by Western blotting and quantified in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: It took 1.0 µM i-CDK9 to cause up to 85% reduction in pSer2
claims.source: It took 1.0 µM i-CDK9 to cause up to 85% reduction in pSer2.
claims.evidence: This is measured by Western blotting and quantification shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: 8-hr incubation with i-CDK9 (0.3 μM) induced the MYC level by 3.3-fold, whereas the same condition reduced the pSer2 level by only 40%
claims.source: In a separate time-course analysis, the 8-hr incubation with i-CDK9 (0.3 μM) induced the MYC level by 3.3-fold, whereas the same condition reduced the pSer2 level by only 40% (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The protein levels are measured by Western blotting and quantified in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: MYC expression was highly responsive to i-CDK9 treatment and occurred at a time point earlier and drug concentration lower than those required to achieve a significant suppression of Ser2 phosphorylation on the Pol II CTD
claims.source: Thus, MYC expression was highly responsive to i-CDK9 treatment and occurred at a time point earlier and drug concentration lower than those required to achieve a significant suppression of Ser2 phosphorylation on the Pol II CTD.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the dose-response and time-course data in Figures 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: Flavopiridol significantly elevated the MYC protein level and this effect required a shorter exposure time (e.g., 4 hr) and lower drug concentration (e.g., 0.1 μM) than those needed to fully reduce the global pSer2 level
claims.source: Just like i-CDK9, flavopiridol also significantly elevated the MYC protein level and this effect required a shorter exposure time (e.g., 4 hr) and lower drug concentration (e.g., 0.1 μM) than those needed to fully reduce the global pSer2 level (Figure 3D,E).
claims.evidence: The protein levels are measured by Western blotting in Figures 3D and 3E.

claims.claim: The nearly identical activities displayed by i-CDK9 and flavopiridol suggest that the inhibition of CDK9 but not some other unknown enzymes was the cause of MYC induction
claims.source: The nearly identical activities displayed by i-CDK9 and flavopiridol, which are very different in their structures, suggest that the inhibition of CDK9 but not some other unknown enzymes was the cause of MYC induction.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the similar effects of two structurally distinct CDK9 inhibitors.

claims.claim: Without cycloheximide pre-treatment, i-CDK9 significantly increased the MYC protein level
claims.source: Without the pre-treatment, i-CDK9 significantly increased the MYC protein level as expected (Figure 3F, lanes 1–2).
claims.evidence: The protein level is measured by Western blotting in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: In the presence of cycloheximide, MYC production was essentially wiped out in both the i-CDK9-treated and i-CDK9-untreated cells
claims.source: In the presence of CHX, however, MYC production was essentially wiped out in both the i-CDK9-treated and i-CDK9-untreated cells (lanes 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: The protein level is measured by Western blotting in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: MYC is a labile protein
claims.source: This result, together with the above demonstration that sustained i-CDK9 treatment dramatically increased the MYC mRNA level (Figure 3A), indicates that MYC is a labile protein
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the cycloheximide experiment showing rapid loss of MYC protein when synthesis is blocked.

claims.claim: The prominent accumulation of MYC in i-CDK9-treated cells was most likely due to its enhanced mRNA production but not protein stability
claims.source: This result, together with the above demonstration that sustained i-CDK9 treatment dramatically increased the MYC mRNA level (Figure 3A), indicates that MYC is a labile protein and that its prominent accumulation in i-CDK9-treated cells was most likely due to its enhanced mRNA production but not protein stability.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combination of mRNA level data and cycloheximide experiment results.

claims.claim: i-CDK9 efficiently induced expression from the endogenous MYC locus
claims.source: Interestingly, although i-CDK9 efficiently induced expression from the endogenous MYC locus, it failed to activate production of the Flag-tagged MYC (MYC-F) from a stably transfected, doxycycline-inducible expression construct driven by the CMV promoter (Figure 3G)
claims.evidence: The differential induction is shown by Western blotting in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: i-CDK9 failed to activate production of Flag-tagged MYC from a stably transfected, doxycycline-inducible expression construct driven by the CMV promoter
claims.source: Interestingly, although i-CDK9 efficiently induced expression from the endogenous MYC locus, it failed to activate production of the Flag-tagged MYC (MYC-F) from a stably transfected, doxycycline-inducible expression construct driven by the CMV promoter (Figure 3G)
claims.evidence: The lack of induction is shown by Western blotting in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: i-CDK9 cannot activate MYC transcription from the heterologous CMV promoter
claims.source: indicating that i-CDK9 cannot activate MYC transcription from this heterologous promoter.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that i-CDK9 induces endogenous MYC but not CMV-driven MYC.

claims.claim: i-CDK9 gradually decreased the amounts of HEXIM1 bound to CDK9-F in a dosage-dependent manner
claims.source: Indeed, i-CDK9 gradually decreased the amounts of HEXIM1 bound to CDK9-F and at the same time increased the BRD4-CDK9-F binding in a dosage-dependent manner (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The protein-protein interactions are measured by co-immunoprecipitation and Western blotting in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: i-CDK9 increased the BRD4-CDK9-F binding in a dosage-dependent manner
claims.source: Indeed, i-CDK9 gradually decreased the amounts of HEXIM1 bound to CDK9-F and at the same time increased the BRD4-CDK9-F binding in a dosage-dependent manner (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The protein-protein interactions are measured by co-immunoprecipitation and Western blotting in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The disruption of 7SK snRNP and formation of BRD4-P-TEFb were highly sensitive to i-CDK9 and required as little as 0.1 μM of the drug
claims.source: Just like the induction of MYC expression (Figure 3B), the disruption of 7SK snRNP and formation of BRD4-P-TEFb were highly sensitive to i-CDK9 and required as little as 0.1 μM of the drug (Figure 4A, compare lane 8 to lane 6).
claims.evidence: The sensitivity is shown by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: At 0.1 μM i-CDK9, the global pSer2 level was only slightly decreased
claims.source: At this concentration, i-CDK9 only slightly decreased the global pSer2 level (Figure 4A, compare between lanes 1 and 3) but began to markedly induce MYC expression (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The pSer2 level is measured by Western blotting in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: i-CDK9 (0.3 μM) induced disruption of 7SK snRNP at a time point (1 hr) that was much earlier than that required to cause about 50% reduction in global pSer2 (8 hr)
claims.source: In a time course analysis, i-CDK9 (0.3 μM)-induced disruption of 7SK snRNP at a time point (1 hr) that was much earlier than that required to cause about 50% reduction in global pSer2 (8 hr; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The time course is shown by co-immunoprecipitation and Western blotting in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The loss of BRD4 dramatically reduced both basal and the i-CDK9-induced MYC protein production
claims.source: The loss of BRD4, verified by Western blotting, dramatically reduced both basal and the i-CDK9-induced MYC protein production (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The effect of BRD4 knockdown is shown by Western blotting in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: JQ1 decreased the associations of both BRD4 and CDK9 with the MYC locus in HeLa cells
claims.source: Consistent with the results obtained in other cell types (Mertz et al., 2011; Zuber et al., 2011), JQ1 decreased the associations of both BRD4 and CDK9 with the MYC locus in HeLa cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The decreased associations are shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and the consistency with other cell types is supported by citations to Mertz et al., 2011 and Zuber et al., 2011.

claims.claim: JQ1 completely abolished the MYC induction by i-CDK9 in HeLa, H1792, and A2058 cells
claims.source: More importantly, JQ1 also completely abolished the MYC induction by i-CDK9 in HeLa (Figure 4C) as well as the lung cancer cell line H1792 and the melanoma cell line A2058 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3)
claims.evidence: The abolishment of MYC induction is shown by Western blotting or qRT-PCR in Figures 4C and 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The control enantiomer of JQ1 was ineffective in abolishing MYC induction by i-CDK9
claims.source: whereas the control enantiomer was ineffective in this regard.
claims.evidence: The lack of effect is shown by Western blotting in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The interaction between BRD4 and acetylated chromatin is required for i-CDK9 to induce MYC expression in diverse cell types
claims.source: These observations, in conjunction with the shBRD4 result above, confirm that the interaction between BRD4 and acetylated chromatin is required for i-CDK9 to induce MYC expression in diverse cell types.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined results of BRD4 knockdown and JQ1 treatment experiments in multiple cell lines.

claims.claim: The overexpressed P-TEFb-interacting domain (PID) of BRD4 efficiently suppressed the i-CDK9-induced MYC protein production
claims.source: Western analyses indicate that the PID efficiently suppressed the induction (Figure 4D, lanes 3 and 4)
claims.evidence: The suppression is shown by Western blotting in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The PID strongly interacted with CDK9 and CycT1 in i-CDK9-treated cells
claims.source: likely due to its own strong interaction with CDK9 and CycT1 in i-CDK9-treated cells (Figure 4E)
claims.evidence: The interaction is shown by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The PID interfered with the interaction of endogenous BRD4 with P-TEFb
claims.source: which in turn interfered with the interaction of endogenous BRD4 with P-TEFb (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The interference is shown by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The overexpressed kinase-inactive CDK9 mutant D167N prevented i-CDK9 from inducing MYC
claims.source: This point is illustrated by the demonstration that the overexpressed kinase-inactive CDK9 mutant D167N, which binds to BRD4-like WT CDK9 (Yang et al., 2005) and acts dominant-negatively to suppress the activity of endogenous CDK9 (Garber et al., 2000), prevented i-CDK9 from inducing MYC (Figure 4D, lanes 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: The prevention is shown by Western blotting in Figure 4D, and the properties of D167N are supported by citations to Yang et al., 2005 and Garber et al., 2000.

claims.claim: The initial MYC induction by a low level (e.g., 0.3 μM) of i-CDK9 was subsequently shut off by a higher i-CDK9 concentration (e.g., 2 μM)
claims.source: The dependence on catalytically active P-TEFb for MYC induction was further demonstrated by the observation that the initial MYC induction by a low level (e.g., 0.3 μM) of i-CDK9 was subsequently shut off by a higher i-CDK9 concentration (e.g., 2 μM, see Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The shut-off is shown by Western blotting in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: No MYC induction was detected when 2 μM i-CDK9 was added into the medium at time zero
claims.source: No MYC induction was detected also when 2 μM i-CDK9 was added into the medium at time zero (see Figure 7A below).
claims.evidence: The lack of induction is shown by Western blotting in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The RNAi-mediated knockdown of cellular CDK9 and CycT1 levels completely abolished the i-CDK9-induced MYC expression
claims.source: Finally, the RNAi-mediated KD of cellular CDK9 and CycT1 levels also completely abolished the i-CDK9-induced MYC expression (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The abolishment is shown by Western blotting in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Knockdown of CDK12 failed to prevent i-CDK9 from inducing MYC
claims.source: In contrast, KD of CDK12, another reported CTD kinase, failed to prevent i-CDK9 from inducing MYC (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: The lack of effect is shown by Western blotting and qRT-PCR in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: The i-CDK9 induction of MYC expression depends on the enhanced interaction of BRD4 with catalytically active P-TEFb released from 7SK snRNP as well as the binding of the BRD4-P-TEFb complex to acetylated MYC chromatin template
claims.source: Taken together, these data strongly support the notion that the i-CDK9 induction of MYC expression depends on the enhanced interaction of BRD4 with catalytically active P-TEFb released from 7SK snRNP as well as the binding of the BRD4-P-TEFb complex to acetylated MYC chromatin template.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined results of multiple experiments including knockdowns, inhibitors, and mutants.

claims.claim: WT BRD4 was able to increase CDK9 kinase activity dose dependently up to 2.2-fold
claims.source: While WT BRD4 was able to increase CDK9 kinase activity dose dependently up to 2.2-fold, ∆PID lacked this ability (Figure 4I)
claims.evidence: The increase in kinase activity is measured by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: BRD4∆PID lacked the ability to increase CDK9 kinase activity
claims.source: While WT BRD4 was able to increase CDK9 kinase activity dose dependently up to 2.2-fold, ∆PID lacked this ability (Figure 4I)
claims.evidence: The lack of effect is shown by in vitro kinase assays in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: The physical interaction between BRD4 and P-TEFb is essential for the elevated CDK9 activity
claims.source: indicating that the physical interaction between BRD4 and P-TEFb was essential for the elevated CDK9 activity.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing the effects of WT BRD4 and ∆PID on CDK9 activity.

claims.claim: Neither WT nor ∆PID BRD4 alone was able to cause phosphorylation of the CTD peptide in the absence of P-TEFb
claims.source: It is worth pointing out that different from a recent study reporting that BRD4 is an atypical kinase that can directly phosphorylate the Pol II CTD on Ser2 (Devaiah et al., 2012), neither WT nor ∆PID BRD4 alone was able to cause phosphorylation of the CTD peptide in the absence of P-TEFb (Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: The lack of kinase activity is shown by in vitro kinase assays in Figure 4I, and the contrast with another study is supported by citation to Devaiah et al., 2012.

claims.claim: BRD4 rendered CDK9 less sensitive to inhibition by i-CDK9
claims.source: In addition to increasing CDK9's catalytic activity, BRD4 was also found to render CDK9 less sensitive to inhibition by i-CDK9, whereas BRD4∆PID was less effective in this regard (Figure 4J).
claims.evidence: The protection against inhibition is shown by in vitro kinase assays with varying i-CDK9 concentrations in Figure 4J.

claims.claim: In the absence of BRD4, it took only 4.4 ± 0.7 nM i-CDK9 to achieve 50% inhibition of CDK9
claims.source: For example, in the absence of BRD4, it took only 4.4 ± 0.7 nM i-CDK9 to achieve 50% inhibition of CDK9 (i.e., IC50 = 4.4 ± 0.7 nM).
claims.evidence: The IC50 is measured by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 4J.

claims.claim: The addition of WT BRD4 into the reaction protected CDK9 against i-CDK9 and increased IC50 to 14.7 ± 2.1 nM
claims.source: However, the addition of WT BRD4 into the reaction protected CDK9 against i-CDK9 and increased IC50 to 14.7 ± 2.1 nM.
claims.evidence: The IC50 is measured by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 4J.

claims.claim: BRD4∆PID changed the IC50 value to 7.2 ± 0.6 nM
claims.source: BRD4∆PID, on the other hand, displayed a much weaker effect by changing the IC50 value to 7.2 ± 0.6 nM (Figure 4J).
claims.evidence: The IC50 is measured by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 4J.

claims.claim: The i-CDK9-mediated MYC induction benefited from efficient release of P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP
claims.source: These data indicate that the i-CDK9-mediated MYC induction benefited not only from efficient release of P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP, but the drug-enhanced BRD4-P-TEFb interaction can also directly promote CDK9's kinase activity and resistance to inhibition, in addition to its recruitment of more P-TEFb to the MYC locus.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined results of co-immunoprecipitation and in vitro kinase assays.

claims.claim: The drug-enhanced BRD4-P-TEFb interaction can directly promote CDK9's kinase activity and resistance to inhibition
claims.source: These data indicate that the i-CDK9-mediated MYC induction benefited not only from efficient release of P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP, but the drug-enhanced BRD4-P-TEFb interaction can also directly promote CDK9's kinase activity and resistance to inhibition, in addition to its recruitment of more P-TEFb to the MYC locus.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the in vitro kinase assays showing BRD4's effects on CDK9 activity and inhibitor sensitivity.

claims.claim: i-CDK9 caused a significant increase in BRD4's occupancy across the entire MYC locus
claims.source: The first noticeable major change caused by i-CDK9 is the significant increase in BRD4's occupancy across the entire MYC locus (Figure 5A,B)
claims.evidence: The increased occupancy is shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figures 5A and 5B.

claims.claim: There was significantly elevated CDK9 binding to the MYC locus upon i-CDK9 treatment
claims.source: Correlating with this increase and consistent with the i-CDK9-induced BRD4-P-TEFb interaction, there was also significantly elevated CDK9 binding to the MYC locus (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The elevated binding is shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The elevation in CDK9 binding to the MYC locus was mostly BRD4 dependent
claims.source: Although the elevation in CDK9 binding was mostly BRD4 dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
claims.evidence: The BRD4 dependence is shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The distribution pattern of CDK9 was somewhat different from that of BRD4 at the MYC locus

results.result: i-CDK9 is a highly selective and potent CDK9 inhibitor with a novel chemical scaffold. It inhibits CDK9-CycT1 with an IC50 below 0.0004 µM and shows >600-fold selectivity over other CDKs (CDK1, CDK2, CDK4, CDK7, CDK8), far superior to flavopiridol's 2.9-28.6-fold selectivity. Among >400 kinases tested, only 9 showed significant binding inhibition, with DYRK1A and DYRK1B being the next best targets at >100-fold lower affinity than CDK9.
results.evaluation: The selectivity and potency claims are well-supported by multiple orthogonal assays (AlphaScreen kinase assay, KINOMEscan binding assay) with consistent results across platforms. The structural distinctiveness is documented, and the co-crystal structure provides mechanistic validation. The comparison to flavopiridol establishes clear superiority in selectivity.

results.result: i-CDK9 displays marked selectivity for CDK9 over CDK12, another Pol II CTD Ser2 kinase. CDK9-F is inhibited with IC50 ~2 nM while CDK12-F shows no obvious inhibition at 80 nM. Using recombinant proteins, CDK9-CycT1 is mostly inhibited at 80 nM while CDK12-CycK requires 640-1200 nM for significant inhibition.
results.evaluation: The differential selectivity is demonstrated through in vitro kinase assays using both affinity-purified and recombinant proteins, with consistent results showing >10-fold selectivity. The comparison to flavopiridol (which shows similar selectivity) provides additional validation through independent literature.

results.result: i-CDK9 elicits cellular responses consistent with P-TEFb inhibition in HeLa cells. It dose-dependently reduces pSer2 on Pol II CTD and pThr775 on SPT5, downregulates the short-lived protein MCL-1, and induces PARP cleavage (a hallmark of apoptosis).
results.evaluation: The cellular effects are demonstrated by Western blotting with dose-response relationships. The observed effects (reduced phosphorylation of known CDK9 substrates, decreased short-lived protein expression, apoptosis markers) are all mechanistically consistent with CDK9 inhibition and provide orthogonal validation of on-target activity.

results.result: i-CDK9 causes genome-wide Pol II pausing at gene promoters. ChIP-seq analysis shows that 56.6% (2 hr) and 68.4% (8 hr) of 11,197 genes with detectable Pol II displayed ≥1.5-fold increase in traveling ratio (TR). Genes with increased TR are enriched for RNA processing and transcription functions, while genes with the largest expression decreases are involved in transcription regulation and RNA metabolism.
results.evaluation: The genome-wide pausing is rigorously demonstrated by ChIP-seq with clear quantitative metrics (TR calculation) and appropriate controls. The GO enrichment analysis provides biological context. However, the claim that genes upregulated ≥2-fold showed significantly less TR change (C27) requires careful interpretation as it represents a small subset (138 genes) with potentially different regulatory mechanisms.

results.result: MYC expression displays a biphasic response to i-CDK9 treatment: initial decrease (within 2 hr) followed by dramatic rebound (8-16 hr). This pattern is observed across five cell lines (HeLa, U87MG, A375, NCIH441, A2058) with varying MYC copy numbers, though the magnitude of initial decrease and subsequent induction varies among cell lines.
results.evaluation: The biphasic response is demonstrated by microarray analysis at multiple time points and confirmed by qRT-PCR. The observation across multiple cell lines with different MYC amplification states strengthens the conclusion that this is a general phenomenon. The variation in magnitude across cell lines is appropriately noted and may reflect differences in mRNA stability.

results.result: HEXIM1, another short-lived gene dependent on CDK9, was continuously suppressed throughout 16 hr of i-CDK9 treatment in all five cell lines, contrasting with MYC's biphasic response.
results.evaluation: The continuous suppression of HEXIM1 is demonstrated by microarray analysis and provides an important control showing that not all CDK9-dependent genes exhibit the biphasic response. The prior literature citation establishes HEXIM1's CDK9 dependence.

results.result: MYC induction by i-CDK9 occurs at lower drug concentrations and earlier time points than required for significant global pSer2 suppression. At 0.1 µM i-CDK9, MYC increased 3.6-fold while global pSer2 decreased only 23%; 1.0 µM was required for 85% pSer2 reduction. Similarly, 8 hr at 0.3 µM induced MYC 3.3-fold while reducing pSer2 only 40%.
results.evaluation: The dose-response and time-course data from Western blotting clearly demonstrate the differential sensitivity. The quantification shows MYC induction occurs before substantial global CDK9 inhibition, which is a key mechanistic insight. The measurements are internally consistent across experiments.

results.result: Flavopiridol, a structurally distinct pan-CDK inhibitor, produces similar MYC induction as i-CDK9, requiring shorter exposure time (4 hr) and lower concentration (0.1 µM) than needed for full global pSer2 reduction. This suggests CDK9 inhibition specifically, not off-target effects, causes MYC induction.
results.evaluation: The parallel effects of two structurally distinct CDK9 inhibitors provide strong evidence that the MYC induction is on-target. This is a critical control that rules out compound-specific artifacts. The dose-response and time-course patterns mirror those of i-CDK9.

results.result: The MYC accumulation in i-CDK9-treated cells is due to enhanced mRNA production rather than increased protein stability. Cycloheximide treatment eliminated MYC protein in both i-CDK9-treated and untreated cells, demonstrating MYC is a labile protein. Combined with the observed mRNA increase, this indicates the mechanism is transcriptional.
results.evaluation: The cycloheximide experiment clearly demonstrates that continuous protein synthesis is required for MYC accumulation, ruling out protein stabilization as the mechanism. Combined with the mRNA data from microarray and qRT-PCR, this provides strong evidence for a transcriptional mechanism.

results.result: i-CDK9 induces expression from the endogenous MYC locus but fails to activate a CMV promoter-driven MYC construct, indicating the induction requires the native MYC promoter context.
results.evaluation: The differential response between endogenous and CMV-driven MYC is clearly demonstrated by Western blotting. This is an important mechanistic insight showing promoter-specific regulation, though the experiment could be strengthened by testing other heterologous promoters.

results.result: i-CDK9 efficiently induces transfer of P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP to BRD4. In a dose-dependent manner, i-CDK9 decreased HEXIM1-CDK9 binding while increasing BRD4-CDK9 binding. This occurred at 0.1 µM (where global pSer2 was only slightly decreased) and as early as 1 hr (much earlier than the 8 hr required for 50% pSer2 reduction at 0.3 µM).
results.evaluation: The P-TEFb redistribution is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation with clear dose-response and time-course relationships. The sensitivity of this redistribution (occurring at low concentrations and early time points) is a key mechanistic finding that helps explain the MYC induction kinetics.

results.result: BRD4 and its interaction with acetylated chromatin are required for i-CDK9-induced MYC expression. BRD4 knockdown dramatically reduced both basal and i-CDK9-induced MYC production. JQ1 (BET bromodomain inhibitor) completely abolished MYC induction by i-CDK9 in HeLa, H1792, and A2058 cells, while the control enantiomer was ineffective.
results.evaluation: The requirement for BRD4 is demonstrated through multiple orthogonal approaches (shRNA knockdown, pharmacological inhibition with JQ1, control enantiomer) across multiple cell lines. The ChIP-qPCR data showing JQ1 reduces BRD4 and CDK9 association with MYC locus provides mechanistic support.

results.result: Catalytically active P-TEFb and its interaction with BRD4 are essential for i-CDK9-induced MYC expression. Overexpressed BRD4-PID suppressed MYC induction by competing with endogenous BRD4 for P-TEFb binding. Kinase-dead CDK9 (D167N) prevented MYC induction. High i-CDK9 concentrations (2 µM) that completely inhibit CDK9 abolished MYC induction. CDK9/CycT1 knockdown eliminated MYC induction, while CDK12 knockdown had no effect.
results.evaluation: The requirement for catalytically active P-TEFb is demonstrated through multiple complementary approaches: dominant-negative PID, kinase-dead mutant, dose-dependent inhibition, and specific knockdowns. The specificity for CDK9 over CDK12 is particularly important given both are CTD kinases. The logic is internally consistent.

results.result: BRD4 directly increases CDK9 kinase activity through physical interaction. WT BRD4 increased CDK9 activity dose-dependently up to 2.2-fold in vitro, while ΔPID (lacking P-TEFb interaction domain) lacked this ability. Neither WT nor ΔPID BRD4 alone could phosphorylate CTD peptide without P-TEFb.
results.evaluation: The in vitro kinase assays with purified components clearly demonstrate BRD4's direct effect on CDK9 activity and the requirement for physical interaction (ΔPID control). The demonstration that BRD4 lacks intrinsic kinase activity is an important control that contradicts a prior report (Devaiah et al., 2012).

results.result: BRD4 renders CDK9 less sensitive to i-CDK9 inhibition. In the absence of BRD4, IC50 for CDK9 inhibition was 4.4 ± 0.7 nM. WT BRD4 increased IC50 to 14.7 ± 2.1 nM (3.3-fold protection), while ΔPID showed weaker protection (IC50 = 7.2 ± 0.6 nM).
results.evaluation: The protection against inhibition is quantitatively demonstrated by in vitro kinase assays with clear IC50 measurements. The ΔPID control shows the effect requires physical interaction. This is a novel finding that helps explain how MYC can be induced despite CDK9 inhibition.

results.result: The i-CDK9-mediated MYC induction benefits from multiple mechanisms: efficient P-TEFb release from 7SK snRNP, BRD4-enhanced CDK9 kinase activity and resistance to inhibition, and BRD4-mediated recruitment of P-TEFb to the MYC locus.
results.evaluation: This integrative conclusion is well-supported by the combination of co-immunoprecipitation data (P-TEFb redistribution), in vitro kinase assays (activity enhancement and protection), and ChIP data (recruitment to MYC locus). The multiple mechanisms work synergistically to explain the paradoxical MYC induction.

results.result: i-CDK9 treatment causes significant increases in BRD4, CDK9, total Pol II, and pSer2 occupancy across the MYC locus. Despite 0.3 µM i-CDK9 for 8 hr reducing global pSer2 by ~40%, pSer2 levels increased at the MYC locus. The CDK9 elevation was mostly BRD4-dependent, though CDK9 and BRD4 showed somewhat different distribution patterns.
results.evaluation: The ChIP-qPCR data clearly demonstrate increased occupancy of key factors at the MYC locus. The local increase in pSer2 despite global decrease is a striking finding that explains the MYC induction. The BRD4 dependence of CDK9 recruitment is appropriately demonstrated. The different distribution patterns are noted but speculatively explained.

results.result: On HEXIM1, a gene permanently inhibited by i-CDK9, treatment decreased levels of both total Pol II and pSer2 Pol II, contrasting with the increases observed at the MYC locus.
results.evaluation: The HEXIM1 data provide an important negative control showing that the effects at MYC are gene-specific rather than global. The ChIP-qPCR data clearly show opposite effects on HEXIM1 versus MYC.

results.result: Acetylated histones H3 and H4 increased across the MYC locus (especially near the P1 promoter) upon i-CDK9 treatment, while global levels in whole cell extracts remained unchanged. This increased acetylation explains the drug-promoted BRD4 binding to the MYC locus.
results.evaluation: The ChIP-qPCR data demonstrate local increases in histone acetylation at MYC despite no global change (Western blot control). The inference that this explains BRD4 recruitment is reasonable given BRD4's known function as an acetyl-lysine reader, though the mechanism causing the acetylation increase is unclear.

results.result: Early chromatin changes (0-2 hr) at MYC versus HEXIM1 promoters predict their divergent responses to i-CDK9. At MYC, Ac-H3 and especially Ac-H4 increased early, and BRD4 showed initial decrease but rebounded by 2 hr. At HEXIM1, Ac-H3 drastically decreased while Ac-H4 slightly increased, and BRD4 showed sustained reduction.
results.evaluation: The time-course ChIP-qPCR data reveal early chromatin differences that precede the divergent transcriptional outcomes. This is an important mechanistic insight, though the interpretation that these differences "predispose" genes to different fates (C99) is somewhat speculative and would benefit from additional validation.

results.result: The i-CDK9-induced MYC expression results from a combination of: (1) induced P-TEFb transfer from 7SK snRNP to BRD4; (2) BRD4's promotion of CDK9 activity and resistance to inhibition; and (3) favorable early chromatin changes leading to increased BRD4-P-TEFb occupancy, enhanced pSer2, and productive elongation at the MYC locus.
results.evaluation: This comprehensive mechanistic model integrates all the major findings from co-IP, in vitro kinase assays, ChIP-qPCR, and expression data. Each component is individually well-supported, and the model provides a coherent explanation for the paradoxical MYC induction during CDK9 inhibition.

results.result: MYC and other BRD4-dependent primary response genes (BDPR genes) show the same biphasic transcriptional response to i-CDK9. GSEA of 27 curated BDPR genes shows marked reduction at 2 hr (NES = -2.28) followed by significant up-regulation at 8 hr (NES = +2.26).
results.evaluation: The GSEA analysis provides rigorous statistical evidence that the biphasic response is not unique to MYC but extends to a defined set of BDPR genes. The gene set is appropriately curated from published literature, and the statistical significance is strong (FDR q-value <0.001).

results.result: The 23 BDPR genes with detectable Pol II ChIP-seq signals showed little change in traveling ratio (TR) after 8 hr i-CDK9 exposure, contrasting with most other genes. ChIP-seq reveals i-CDK9 caused significant and fairly uniform Pol II increase across the entire length of MYC, FOS, and JUNB, explaining why their TR values changed little.
results.evaluation: The ChIP-seq data clearly show that BDPR genes behave differently from most genes in terms of TR changes. The uniform Pol II increase across gene length (rather than just promoter-proximal accumulation) logically explains the minimal TR change. The consistency between ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR for MYC validates the approach.

results.result: The induced P-TEFb transfer from 7SK snRNP to BRD4 and BRD4-mediated protection/enhancement of P-TEFb activity and recruitment to chromatin are the primary driving forces behind i-CDK9 induction of MYC and other BDPR genes.
results.evaluation: This summary conclusion integrates the mechanistic findings and is well-supported by the totality of evidence from co-IP, in vitro kinase assays, ChIP experiments, and expression analyses. The conclusion appropriately synthesizes the major findings.

results.result: MYC is required for CDK9 to phosphorylate Pol II CTD under both normal and inhibitory conditions. Incomplete MYC knockdown markedly reduced pSer2 levels in both untreated cells and cells exposed to a range of i-CDK9 concentrations.
results.evaluation: The MYC knockdown experiment clearly demonstrates MYC's role in facilitating CDK9 function. The effect is observed across a range of i-CDK9 concentrations, strengthening the conclusion. However, the knockdown is incomplete, which somewhat limits the interpretation.

results.result: MYC normally facilitates P-TEFb's phosphorylation of Pol II CTD on Ser2. JQ1 and 10,058-F4 (MYC-MAX inhibitor) each slightly decreased cellular pSer2 levels. When combined with i-CDK9, both caused much greater pSer2 reduction than i-CDK9 alone, indicating that decreasing MYC expression or activity eliminates its beneficial effect on P-TEFb function.
results.evaluation: The combination experiments with two different approaches to inhibit MYC (BRD4 inhibition reducing MYC expression, and direct MYC-MAX inhibition) both show synergistic effects with i-CDK9 on pSer2 reduction. This provides strong evidence for MYC's role in facilitating P-TEFb function through multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: MYC recruits P-TEFb to target genes, and i-CDK9 treatment increases MYC's interaction with CDK9, CycT1, and BRD4. This reveals a dual compensatory mechanism: cells respond to CDK9 inhibition by both increasing MYC expression and enhancing MYC's recruitment of the BRD4-P-TEFb complex to essential genes.
results.evaluation: The co-immunoprecipitation data clearly show increased MYC-P-TEFb interaction upon i-CDK9 treatment. The interpretation as a compensatory mechanism is well-reasoned and supported by the prior literature on MYC's ability to recruit P-TEFb. The dual mechanism (increased expression + increased interaction) is a key insight.

results.result: Simultaneous inhibition of CDK9 and MYC/BRD4 synergistically induces growth arrest and apoptosis in cancer cells. i-CDK9 combined with JQ1 synergistically inhibited growth and induced apoptosis (measured by Caspase 3/7 and sub-G1 population) in HeLa and H1792 cells. The MYC inhibitor 10,058-F4 also synergized with i-CDK9 to induce cell death.
results.evaluation: The synergy is rigorously demonstrated using isobologram analysis (the appropriate method for assessing drug interactions) across multiple cell lines and with multiple readouts (proliferation, caspase activation, DNA fragmentation). The use of two different approaches to target MYC (JQ1 and 10,058-F4) strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: CDK9 is the kinase subunit of P-TEFb that enables Pol II's transition from promoter-proximal pausing to productive elongation.
results.evaluation: This is well-established background knowledge appropriately stated in the abstract. It provides necessary context for the study.

results.result: The study establishes that i-CDK9 potently suppresses CDK9 activity and causes genome-wide Pol II pausing, but MYC and other primary response genes paradoxically increase expression through a BRD4-dependent mechanism. Because this compensatory MYC induction limits the efficacy of CDK9 inhibition alone, simultaneous inhibition of CDK9 and MYC/BRD4 is required for efficient cancer cell killing.
results.evaluation: This abstract summary accurately captures the major findings of the study. Each component is well-supported by the detailed results. The therapeutic implication (combinatorial strategy) logically follows from the mechanistic findings and synergy data.
